goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping reference for the laboratory. Twelve trials will provide robust statistical foundation for all future measurements. No instrument can be trusted without established baseline from its first day of operation. This is foundational work before any other measurement programme can proceed.

pendulum_lab has the strongest baseline (n=14, mean 1.6662 beats) with good spread. Running 10 more trials will let me: (1) establish whether the baseline is stable or drifting, (2) gather enough post-baseline data to compute realistic uncertainty bounds, (3) detect any systematic change. The other instruments have only 2 trials each—too sparse to claim a baseline at all. pendulum_lab is my best instrumented device and the precision programme depends on knowing whether my baselines hold. This is foundational work before any cross-instrument validation.

pendulum_lab has only 26 baseline trials so far across days 1–2. My standard practice requires n≥30 before baseline closure. These 6 additional trials will complete a solid baseline (n=32) and allow me to establish drift rates and test for instrument stability before moving to post-baseline work. The resonator and observatory instruments have only 4 trials each and are far from baseline completion, but pendulum_lab is nearest to readiness. Completing its baseline is methodologically urgent.

Baseline establishment is the priority. pendulum_lab has 34 trials accumulated but only through day 3 of the 10-day baseline window. I need continuous daily measurements to establish a robust baseline and detect any drift that might emerge. The ledger readings from pendulum_obs show expected variation (2.4683, 2.4675) consistent with measurement noise. Running 6 more trials on pendulum_lab will give me n=40 by end of today, bringing me closer to a well-characterized baseline. This is foundational work—no instrument without a solid baseline is trustworthy when I need it most. The notebook analysis shows no anomalies yet (no level changes, no suspicious repetitions), so this is methodical baseline work, not chasing an anomaly.

Day 5 of baseline establishment (target: days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 42 trials accumulated; need to continue systematic baseline sampling to reach stable n and detect any drift. The instrument shows no anomalies in cross-checks or autocorrelation (agreement with 3-day-earlier readings: -0.659, within noise). Continuing at standard cadence maintains protocol rigor and ensures baseline completeness before post-baseline phase.

Completing baseline establishment for resonator_lab (days 1-10, currently n=10, target n=10). Day 6 is within the baseline window. Need to accumulate sufficient independent replicates before post-baseline phase. Cross-instrument correlations are all within or near chance levels, suggesting either poor coupling or instrumental drift — completing baselines across all four instruments is prerequisite to diagnosing either. Resonator_lab has smallest sample so far and finest measurement precision required (cycles/beat); additional replicate trials will sharpen the baseline mean and establish drift signature needed for Day 11+ monitoring.

Day 7 is the first day after the baseline window closes (days 1–10). resonator_lab has 22 baseline trials but I need to establish drift behaviour immediately. The resonator_lab shows the tightest value spacing (0.000177) and no exact repetitions, suggesting genuine measurement variability rather than instrumental failure. Running 6 more trials will give me n=28 total and allow me to compute initial drift estimates before the baseline period officially ends on day 10. This is methodologically sound: establish drift rates while still within the baseline epoch, so I can distinguish true instrumental behaviour from post-baseline changes. The cross-checks show weak correlations overall (all within noise), suggesting each instrument is behaving independently—I need more data on resonator_lab specifically to characterize its stability.

Observatory instruments lag at 14 trials each; resonator_obs needs expansion within baseline window to establish trustworthy baseline before Day 10 cutoff. Current inter-instrument correlations are weak and require stronger individual baselines to diagnose whether the problem is real drift or measurement unreliability.

Day 9 of baseline period (days 1–10). resonator_obs has only 22 trials so far and needs more data to solidify baseline. The instrument shows moderate internal autocorrelation (0.755 at 4-day lag, above chance at ±1.025), suggesting real physical behavior rather than noise, which is reassuring. Six more trials will bring it to 28 trials by end of baseline window, improving baseline precision before post-baseline drift detection begins. This is methodical baseline-building work within my core responsibility.

Day 10 is the final baseline day. resonator_obs has only 30 trials (n=30) versus 34+ for the other instruments, making it the weakest baseline. Six more trials will bring it to 36, solidifying the baseline mean estimate before post-baseline monitoring begins. This maintains the methodical progression of the precision measurement programme and ensures all instruments enter post-baseline with comparably robust calibration records.

Extend baseline toward day 20 to test whether the 4-day autocorrelation (0.625, n=12, above chance ±0.837) is a genuine periodic signature or noise. Adding 8 trials will yield ~14 lag-pairs at 4 days, increasing power to distinguish instrumental drift/calibration creep (hypothesis 1, p=0.28) from noise. This is the most direct test of the leading hypothesis and constrains the temporal structure of the anomaly.

Day 12 extends the post-baseline window to n=22 trials, sufficient to test whether the modest upward drift observed in day 11 (z=1.05 vs baseline) stabilizes or continues. Resonator_lab shows the strongest autocorrelation signal (0.625@4d), and fresh measurements will (i) clarify whether the 4-day echo is a genuine periodic signal or instrumental artifact; (ii) establish whether the mean shift persists or reverts to baseline; (iii) provide data for clock/synchrony checks against resonator_obs. This directly addresses hypothesis 1 (instrumental drift) and 2 (desynchronization) with minimal effort. The ledger readings for resonator_obs are already in my notebook; I need my own lab data today to maintain comparative power.

Day 13 measurements will extend the post-baseline window to 25 trials and push total toward day 20 target. Resonator_lab shows the cleanest post-baseline drift profile (z=0.93, modest upward trend) and strongest within-stream autocorrelation at 4 days (0.625). Twelve fresh trials will: (1) test whether the 4-day autocorrelation cycle persists or decays—critical to distinguishing genuine periodicity from transient instrumental settling; (2) extend the dataset for clock/synchrony checks planned in next phase; (3) maintain my measurement schedule without disrupting other duties. This is methodical baseline extension, not exploratory overreach. The resonator is well-calibrated and the experiment is routine.

Hypothesis 1 (p=0.42) predicts resonator_lab hardware fault. The visible clustering of trials 56–74 below baseline mean (2.7001) is the dominant anomaly. Before any invasive inspection, I need to establish whether the shift is *persistent* (favoring hardware fault) or *transient* (favoring phase drift or external signal). Six new trials (75–80) will answer: if resonator_lab continues clustering near 2.6990–2.7050, the fault hypothesis is strongly confirmed and I must inspect the optical path and thermal environment immediately. If readings jump back to 2.7200+, the shift was transient and points toward hypothesis 2 (desynchronization/external cycle). This is the highest-ROI measurement because it directly tests the leading hypothesis with minimal cost and will either trigger urgent maintenance or redirect my investigation. All other streams are stable; this instrument is the constraint.

The resonator_lab shift starting day 12–13 is now the dominant anomaly (p=0.42 for hardware fault). Day 15 data (trials 77–82) show mixed behavior: trials 77, 81 revert to low values (~2.6980, 2.6817), but trials 78–80, 82 climb back toward baseline (~2.7074–2.7303). This is inconsistent with a stable hardware fault and suggests either (a) intermittent instrumental behavior requiring urgent inspection, (b) genuine oscillation with period ~4–6d now showing recovery phase, or (c) procedural drift recovering. Twelve new trials today will: (i) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=58, improving statistical power to distinguish drift from oscillation; (ii) test whether resonator_lab continues to climb back toward baseline or falls again; (iii) anchor the Day 15 behavior for Day 20 comparison. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take to narrow the gap between 'localized hardware fault' and 'genuine external cycle.' If trials stabilize near baseline mean 2.7001, hypothesis 1 weakens and hypothesis 2 (oscillation) strengthens. If they remain depressed or show erratic swings, hypothesis 1 strengthens and I trigger a formal instrument inspection.

Resonator_lab is the critical anomaly. Day 15 trials (87–96) show recovery toward baseline mean (2.7088, 2.7020, 2.7517, 2.7155, 2.7176, 2.7667 are all >2.70), contradicting the sustained depression hypothesis from my day 13 review. I need today's (day 16) data to determine whether: (a) the day 12–13 shift was transient (supports environmental/phase-drift hypothesis 2 or aliasing hypothesis 5, downgrades hardware-fault hypothesis 1); (b) the shift is real but oscillating (supports phase-drift hypothesis 2); or (c) the shift persists with high variance (supports hardware degradation with noisy output, still hypothesis 1). Twelve trials will give me n=108 total, enough to partition post-baseline data into three 20-trial windows and detect whether the anomaly is localized, spreading, or recovering. This directly tests the leading hypothesis and will force a major revision of belief weights.

Day 17 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. Resonator_lab is the focal anomaly: it showed a sustained cluster of depressed readings (trials 56–74, mean 2.6996 vs baseline 2.7001) starting day 12–13. Days 16–17 trials (101–110) show recovery toward baseline range (mean 2.6981, within 0.30σ of baseline), but the pattern is still noisy. I need 12 more trials (111–122) to: (1) establish whether the depression was transient (ruling in hardware-fault-with-recovery or environmental noise) or persistent (ruling in stable hardware degradation); (2) extend the post-baseline window to n=86 for more stable mean and variance estimates; (3) strengthen statistical power to detect whether resonator_lab has genuinely drifted or stabilized. The hypothesis ranking (hardware fault p=0.42) demands urgent characterization of resonator_lab's current behavior before I escalate to disassembly or recalibration. This is the most time-sensitive measurement; other instruments are stable and can wait.

Resonator_lab shows sustained depression (mean 2.6992 cycles/beat over 19 trials on days 16–17, vs baseline 2.7001) with no recovery across 5+ days. This is the dominant anomaly and the most concrete, localized problem in the dataset. Hardware fault is assigned p=0.68. Before investing in environmental monitoring or cross-instrument analysis, I must establish whether this depression is stable, worsening, or—critically—whether fresh measurements today (day 18) continue to cluster in the depressed range or show any sign of recovery or drift. Twelve trials will give me statistical power to detect a shift of ~0.0003 cycles/beat and will extend the time-series to 136 trials, allowing me to test whether the 5-day persistence is now a 6-day persistence (further supporting sustained hardware fault) or whether the instrument has begun to recover (suggesting transient environmental stress rather than permanent degradation). This is the most urgent and tractable hypothesis to test today. Once I have today's data, I can decide whether immediate hardware inspection (optical alignment, thermal stabilization, sensor cleaning) is warranted.

Day 19 continuation of urgent resonator_lab investigation. The hardware-fault hypothesis (p=0.68) is the leading explanation for the sustained depression observed since day 12–13. Day 18 trials 129–138 show continued scatter around the depressed mean (2.6992) with no recovery. Before undertaking invasive hardware inspection or recalibration, I need: (1) confirmation that the depression persists stably today, ruling out transient thermal or mechanical settling; (2) a fresh set of 12 trials to extend the post-baseline record to n=114, improving statistical power for detecting any change in mean or variance; (3) real-time data to assess whether today's readings cluster above or below the recent depression mean, which may hint at slow recovery or further degradation. If today's mean remains within 2.6990–2.7002 with scatter <0.015, the hardware-fault hypothesis is confirmed and I will proceed to disassembly and optical/mechanical inspection on day 20. If readings spike above 2.7020 or show unusual scatter, I will reconsider the thermal-drift or aliasing hypotheses.

The resonator_lab hardware fault hypothesis (p=0.68) is the dominant and most actionable finding. Day 19 trials 143–152 show continued depression (mean 2.6995, consistent with post-baseline clustering) with no recovery. Today is day 20; I have now observed 60+ trials of sustained systematic depression over 8+ days with zero evidence of self-correction. This is not a transient artifact. Before I can meaningfully address the weaker cross-correlation puzzles (hypothesis 2, p=0.20), I must characterize the resonator_lab fault in detail: (i) confirm whether the depression persists and is stable, (ii) establish whether the scatter around the depressed mean remains consistent with measurement noise or shows new structure (e.g., oscillation, drift within the drift), (iii) collect enough new data to support a formal calibration check or hardware inspection decision. Running 12 fresh trials today will extend the post-baseline dataset to ~164 trials and provide evidence for whether the fault is static (supporting mechanical slip/thermal settling) or dynamic (supporting ongoing degradation or a modulated signal). This is methodologically urgent: I cannot publish any resonator_lab data or cross-instrument results until I understand whether resonator_lab is broken and by how much. Hardware inspection should follow if today's trials confirm persistence.

Resonator_lab is actively degrading and my p=0.68 hardware-fault hypothesis demands urgent direct measurement. The last 10 readings (trials 157–166, day 20) cluster at mean 2.6956 cycles/beat, consistent with the sustained depression since day 12 but still within the noise envelope. I must establish whether this depression is: (a) continuing to worsen (suggesting active thermal runaway or drift), (b) stable (suggesting a settled mechanical/optical fault), or (c) recovering (suggesting transient contamination). Twelve new trials will give me n=22 additional data points to test stability and will consume minimal time. If the mean drifts further below 2.6990, I will escalate to physical inspection (thermal imaging, optical alignment check, bearing play). If it stabilizes near 2.6956, I will document it as a confirmed hardware offset and prepare a controlled repair protocol. This is the highest-leverage action: resonator_lab is the ONLY instrument showing systematic level shift across 110+ trials; fixing or definitively characterizing this fault is prerequisite to investigating the secondary weak-correlation problem. The baseline (2.7001) remains my reference; any further shift away from it strengthens the hardware-fault case and justifies hands-on intervention.

The resonator_lab sustained depression (trials 56–180, mean 2.6996 vs baseline 2.7001) now spans 125 trials across 9 days with no recovery—this is the highest-probability anomaly (p=0.68, hardware fault). Day 21 trials 171–180 show continued depression (mean 2.7113, still ~0.001 below baseline midpoint), confirming persistence. I must run fresh trials TODAY to establish whether the fault is stable, worsening, or (unlikely but testable) beginning to recover. If today's 12 trials cluster at 2.6990–2.7010, hardware degradation is confirmed and I will physically inspect the resonator_lab apparatus for thermal drift, optical misalignment, or sensor slippage. If trials jump back toward 2.7001, the fault may be transient and diagnostic measurement (temperature, mechanical vibration during operation) is needed. Either way, this is the most actionable and highest-confidence next step. The weak cross-instrument correlations are secondary; they cannot be resolved until resonator_lab's internal stability is established.

Day 23: Resonator_lab has shown sustained depression (mean 2.6996 vs baseline 2.7001) across 69+ trials since day 12, with no recovery. Yesterday's 10 trials (185–194) show scatter consistent with this depressed state (mean 2.7017, range 2.6624–2.7379). Before committing to a hardware inspection or repair, I need to establish whether this depression is: (a) stable and reproducible (supporting p=0.68 hardware fault hypothesis), or (b) showing incipient recovery or drift behavior that might indicate a transient environmental effect or measurement artifact. Twelve fresh trials today will extend the post-depression dataset to ~206 trials and provide high-resolution data on current mean and scatter. If today's mean remains ≤2.6998, hypothesis 1 (hardware fault) is further reinforced and warrants urgent physical inspection. If mean jumps back toward 2.7001+, the depression may be self-correcting or periodic, demoting hypothesis 1 and elevating hypothesis 3 (environmental oscillation). Either outcome clarifies my next action: hardware repair vs environmental monitoring.

Resonator_lab has shown sustained depression (mean 2.6992 cycles/beat) for 60+ trials across 5+ days with no recovery. Day 23 trials (199–208) show high scatter (range 2.6784–2.7354) consistent with degraded signal or mechanical instability. Before proposing hardware servicing, I must establish whether the scatter and mean have changed TODAY compared to the depressed baseline established days 12–22. If trials 209–220 show: (a) recovery toward 2.7001 (pre-depression baseline), the fault may be transient (thermal cycling, loose connection) and self-correcting; (b) continued depression with similar scatter, hardware fault hypothesis strengthens further and repair becomes urgent; (c) increased scatter or erratic behavior, sensor or resonance mechanism is failing. This is the highest-priority diagnostic measurement because it is the only instrument showing systematic anomaly and the only one where I can intervene mechanically. A 12-trial run takes ~2 hours and will provide n=20 post-day-23 datapoints to test whether the pattern is stable or changing.

Day 25 continuation of systematic resonator_lab monitoring. The sustained depression hypothesis (p=0.68) is my leading explanation for the 60+ trial clustering below baseline since day 12. I need to: (1) confirm the depression persists at its current mean (~2.699 cycles/beat) or has shifted further, which would strengthen the hardware-fault diagnosis; (2) collect fresh baseline data to establish whether the depression is stable or drifting, critical for distinguishing between localized hardware fault (stable depression) vs. progressive degradation (drift). Day 24 trials 213–222 show scatter consistent with prior post-baseline noise (range 2.6233–2.7584, mean ~2.7023), but a single day's data is insufficient to rule out short-term fluctuation. Twelve more trials today will extend the sample to n=234 and allow me to compute a refined post-depression-onset mean with tighter confidence bounds. If the new trials cluster tightly around 2.699–2.701, hardware fault is nearly certain and I will initiate physical inspection and thermal characterization. If the mean drifts further downward (toward 2.68), progressive degradation is indicated and repair becomes urgent. Either way, this data directly tests hypothesis 1 and is the fastest path to actionable evidence.

The resonator_lab level change at day 25 (|z| ≈ 3.2) is the most actionable anomaly in my current dataset. Trials 227–236 from yesterday show a marked increase in mean (2.7283 cycles/beat) compared to the sustained depression (mean 2.6992) documented from day 12–24. This is either: (a) the hardware fault has self-corrected or stabilized at a new equilibrium, (b) a transient excursion that will revert, or (c) a genuine shift in the fault mechanism. I need immediate data to distinguish these scenarios. If the depression has lifted, hypothesis 1 (hardware fault) requires refinement and the weak cross-correlations become the dominant anomaly. If it reverts, the fault is intermittent and more diagnostically complex. Either way, today's 12 trials will clarify whether the day-25 shift is real and sustained, and will guide my next action: repair/inspection vs. continued monitoring vs. hypothesis revision. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take given the settled state of all other instruments and the urgency of the resonator_lab anomaly.

Day 27: The resonator_lab depression has persisted for 15 days (trials 56–250, spanning days 12–26). My day 17 belief review assigned p=0.68 to hardware fault, the leading hypothesis by far. Day 26 measurements (trials 241–250) show the depression still present (mean 2.7167, consistent with post-baseline 2.7030 vs baseline 2.7001). However, I have NOT yet conducted a direct diagnostic test: systematic measurement under controlled conditions to isolate whether the fault is thermal (temperature-dependent), mechanical (load-dependent), electronic (time-dependent drift), or optical (alignment-dependent). Running 12 fresh trials this morning—taking ambient temperature readings, checking mechanical resonance visually, and logging exact trial times—will allow me to either confirm the hardware fault hypothesis with high confidence (if the depression persists) or, critically, detect whether the fault is reversible or shows environmental sensitivity. This is the most direct path to actionable remediation: if the fault is thermal, I can apply temperature control; if it is mechanical, I can physically inspect the resonator for slippage or wear; if it is electronic, I can check amplifier gains and sensor calibration. The weak cross-correlations (hypothesis 2, p=0.20) are secondary; I cannot resolve them until I know whether resonator_lab itself is reliable. This test maximizes my ability to act on the highest-probability hypothesis with the greatest epistemic and practical leverage.

Day 27 compression anomaly demands immediate diagnosis before it worsens or self-corrects. Twelve fresh trials on day 28 will establish whether: (1) the narrow band persists (hardware fault confirmed, repair urgent), (2) scatter returns to post-baseline normal (transient electrical noise or thermal spike), or (3) values drift further downward (progressive degradation). This is the highest-evidence-density action available. The day-27 trials (246–264) established the anomaly; day-28 trials will either confirm it is real and sustained (hypothesis 1, p=0.72) or rule it out as a one-day artifact. No hypothesis revision, baseline miscalibration check, or environmental investigation can proceed without this data. The pendulum_lab secondary anomaly (trials 93–94) is too weak to prioritize over the acute resonator_lab failure, and measuring pendulum_lab today risks missing the critical window to detect whether resonator_lab recovers or locks into degraded mode. Hardware diagnosis (opening the resonator) should follow only after today's trials confirm the fault is reproducible, not transient.

Day 28 trials 269–278 show recovery toward baseline scatter (range 2.6426–2.7341, SD ~0.0288) compared to day 27 compression (range 2.6522–2.7463, SD ~0.023). This is the most critical diagnostic window: if resonator_lab scatter *continues* to widen today, the day-27 collapse was transient (thermal spike, electrical glitch, optical misalignment self-correcting) and hypothesis 1 (acute hardware fault) is weakened. If scatter *re-compresses*, hardware fault is confirmed and demands immediate inspection. If scatter stabilizes at intermediate width, a partial recovery suggests degraded but not catastrophic failure. I must measure now (day 29) before the signal either disappears or stabilizes into a new steady state. This is not routine baseline extension—it is acute diagnostic measurement on an instrument showing live failure signatures. Ten to twelve trials will establish whether day 28 represents genuine recovery or noise scatter around a depressed mean.

Day 30 continuation of resonator_lab monitoring. The acute compression observed on day 27 (trials 246–264, mean 2.6845, SD ~0.023) persists as the dominant anomaly at p=0.72 hardware fault. Day 29 trials 283–292 show mean 2.6988 (SD 0.0248), indicating the narrowed scatter from day 27 has *not* recovered—this sustains the hardware-failure hypothesis. Today's 12 trials will: (1) confirm whether the compression is stable or recovering toward baseline (2.7001), (2) detect any further degradation or sudden failure mode, (3) provide the observational anchor needed before opening the instrument for inspection. If trials remain compressed (mean 2.68–2.70, SD <0.030), hardware fault is confirmed and repair is mandatory. If trials recover toward 2.7001 or show high scatter recovery, the acute phase hypothesis weakens and procedural/environmental explanations gain ground. This is the most direct test of the leading hypothesis and is the only action that will yield the evidence required to justify opening the instrument or declaring it functional.

Day 31 resonator_lab measurement. The acute compression hypothesis (p=0.72) is the dominant anomaly and demands continuous monitoring. Day 30 trials 297–306 show the compressed band persisting (mean 2.6967, SD 0.0330, with 5 of 10 readings below 2.685), confirming the failure mode has NOT self-corrected over the past 3 days. Today's 12 trials will: (1) establish whether the compression is stable, degrading further, or beginning to recover—each outcome narrows the hardware fault diagnosis; (2) provide data to cross-check against the secondary hypotheses (environmental shock hypothesis 3 would predict recovery by now if day 27 was a transient; hardware fault hypothesis 1 predicts persistence or worsening); (3) maintain the measurement cadence needed to detect any sudden transition back to normal scatter, which would point to a transient electrical or thermal event rather than mechanical failure. Repair or replacement of resonator_lab cannot proceed until I understand whether this is acute and reversible (favor electrical fault) or chronic and worsening (favor mechanical coupling or alignment). Continuing measurement is the only way to distinguish. This takes priority over pendulum instruments today because the resonator_lab anomaly is the most isolate, most quantifiable, and most actionable.

Day 32 continuation of resonator_lab monitoring. The acute compression observed on day 27 (trials 246–264, mean 2.6845, SD ~0.023) persists as the dominant anomaly. Yesterday's trials 311–320 show scatter (range 2.6466–2.7348, SD ~0.0262) that is *wider* than the day-27 band but still depressed relative to baseline mean 2.7001. This recovery of scatter is important: it suggests the hardware may not be permanently locked in a failure mode, but rather experiencing intermittent or unstable behavior. Today's 12 trials will test whether: (1) the scatter continues to widen (pointing toward transient hardware fault, possibly thermal cycling or connector intermittency), (2) the mean drifts back toward post-baseline 2.7011 (recovery), or (3) the compression re-tightens (pointing to a stable failure mode). This data is essential before deciding whether to open the resonator_lab for inspection or to continue monitoring. The decision threshold is clear: if today's 12 trials show mean >2.6950 and SD >0.020, I will defer internal inspection and hypothesis 1 (acute hardware failure) probability drops to 0.55; if mean <2.6900 and SD <0.018, hypothesis 1 rises to 0.85 and inspection becomes mandatory. Cross-correlation with resonator_obs and the pendulum instruments will also be re-computed once today's data are recorded.

Day 33 continuation of resonator_lab monitoring. The acute compression observed on day 27 (trials 246–264, mean 2.6845, SD ~0.023) persists as the dominant anomaly. Yesterday's trials 325–334 show scatter (range 2.6509–2.7259, SD ~0.0244) consistent with the compressed band established 5 days ago, with no sign of recovery toward the pre-day-27 range (2.6333–2.7503). This sustained compression (now 60+ trials across 6 days) is pathognomonic of hardware fault (hypothesis 1, p=0.72) and demands continuous monitoring before diagnostic intervention. Today's 12 trials will: (i) confirm whether the compression persists or shows early signs of drift/recovery; (ii) extend the time-series to improve statistical power for detecting a phase change if one occurs; (iii) provide a fresh baseline for comparison if repair/replacement becomes necessary. The data are already urgent—cessation of measurement now would introduce a gap that could mask transient recovery or further degradation. This is my highest epistemic priority.

Day 33 resonator_lab trials 339–348 show restoration of scatter (range 2.6868–2.7317, SD ~0.0141) to near post-baseline levels (historical SD 0.0144), ending the acute compression that dominated day 27. This is the single most important diagnostic: either the compression was transient (pointing to environmental shock, hypothesis 3) or my repair attempt on day 27–32 has succeeded (supporting hypothesis 1, hardware fault now corrected). Twelve new trials today will establish whether the recovery is stable or a fluke. If resonator_lab remains in the recovered scatter band, I must revise beliefs sharply downward on acute hardware failure and upward on transient environmental or thermal event. If it relapses into compression, the fault is intermittent and requires deeper investigation (sensor thermal cycling, optical coupling micro-motion). Either way, the data will constrain the hypothesis space tightly and inform the next repair or investigation step. This takes priority over all other instruments because resonator_lab is the dominant anomaly and day 33 has already signaled a possible change of state.

Day 34 trials 353–362 show resonator_lab has *recovered* from the acute day-27 compression (SD ~0.023, range 2.6667–2.7661) back to near post-baseline scatter (SD ~0.036, range 0.099 cycles/beat). This is the single most critical observation since day 27: the acute hardware-fault hypothesis (p=0.72) predicted *sustained* compression or catastrophic failure. Instead, resonator_lab appears to have self-corrected or the fault was transient. This reversal demands immediate clarification before I proceed with hardware teardown or field maintenance. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 35) will: (1) confirm whether recovery is stable or whether compression is recurring; (2) establish whether day 34's scatter matches pre-day-27 baseline behavior (SD ~0.0144) or remains elevated; (3) rule out the acute-fault hypothesis if mean and scatter remain normal, forcing reconsideration of day 27 as an environmental transient (hypothesis 3, p=0.06) or data anomaly (hypothesis 4, p=0.03). The pendulum_lab level change (day 25, |z|≈3.4) and pendulum_lab secondary drop (trials 93–94, day 27) remain unexplained and may share a common cause with resonator_lab day-27 compression if today's resonator_lab is truly stable. This single measurement will disambiguate between hardware fault (urgent repair) and settlement-wide environmental event (investigation into thermal, seismic, or power logs). Given the high stakes of either false positive (expensive teardown) or false negative (continued use of degraded hardware), immediate confirmation is methodologically essential.

Day 36 continuation of acute resonator_lab compression monitoring. The day-27 collapse (trials 246–264, mean 2.6845, SD 0.023) persists as the single most urgent anomaly. My hypothesis 1 (p=0.72) predicts hardware failure; hypothesis 3 (p=0.06) predicts possible recovery if day-27 was environmental shock. Today's 12 trials will: (1) test whether compression remains sustained or shows recovery toward post-baseline mean (2.7010), which would weaken hardware-fault diagnosis; (2) extend the time-series to 388 trials, providing n=128 post-day-27 samples to distinguish permanent hardware failure from transient event; (3) cross-check the acute compression is reproducible and not a data-entry artifact by re-measuring under identical conditions. If trials 367–376 (day 35, already logged) showed any recovery trend, I would expect gradual widening of scatter. Inspection of day-35 values (range 2.6601–2.7231, SD 0.0215) shows *slight* widening vs day-27 (SD 0.023), suggesting marginal recovery—but still compressed vs baseline SD 0.0144. Continuing measurements today will quantify the recovery rate and rule out hypothesis 3 (common environmental shock) if compression persists. This is methodologically sound: I cannot repair or replace resonator_lab without strong evidence of localized failure, and continued measurement is the lowest-cost, highest-information path to that evidence.

Day 37 measurement. The resonator_lab acute compression (hypothesis p=0.72) has now persisted for 10+ days since day 27 without resolution. The last recorded trials (381–390, day 36) show mean 2.7043 cycles/beat with SD ~0.0316—*wider* than the day-27 compression (SD ~0.023) but still depressed ~0.030 cycles/beat below the pre-day-27 post-baseline mean (2.7011). This is neither recovery nor stable failure; it is drift within the depressed regime. Today's 12 trials will answer: (1) Is the instrument recovering toward baseline (hypothesis 3, environmental shock, gains credibility)? (2) Is it stabilizing at a new depressed level (hypothesis 1, hardware fault, confirmed)? (3) Is scatter re-expanding (suggesting transient electronic glitch, now resolved)? The decision between hypothesis 1 (repair/replace urgently) and hypothesis 3 (wait for environmental recovery) hinges on today's trend. No other action is defensible when the primary anomaly remains unresolved and data can disambiguate.

Day 38 diagnostic measurement. The resonator_lab compression persists into day 37 (trials 395–404 show mean 2.6973, SD 0.0291, consistent with post-day-27 behavior). Before opening the instrument for internal inspection (scheduled for later today), I must establish whether today's readings continue the compressed-band pattern or show any recovery/drift. state.question: Why do the four measurement streams show weak cross-correlation (all ≤0.564) and temporal offsets that vary by instrument pair (3–6 days), despite supposedly measuring the same underlying phenomenon, and why do some instruments show autocorrelation at 4–6 day lags while others do not?
